Why TSM rather than a chip designer: TSMC doesn't bet on which AI company wins. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Google, Amazon — they all *design* chips, then hand the blueprint to TSMC to actually manufacture, because essentially nobody else on earth can make them at the leading edge. It's the only toll bridge into the city. Whichever car wins the race, it pays the same toll.

The mechanism is brutally simple. A human warehouse worker costs roughly **$34,000 a year** with benefits. A robot costs roughly **$3,000 a year** in maintenance and electricity. Amazon has over 1.5 million employees and is building 100 new robotic fulfilment centres over 18 months. Robotic facilities process orders **40% faster**. Morgan Stanley puts the annual saving at up to **$4 billion**.

> **If I had to put my own money in one name on this question: META.**
>
> It is the only company on earth that has published a quarter where revenue grew 28% and the human headcount went *down* — and the market is charging you 17.6 times forward earnings for it, cheaper than Microsoft, cheaper than Amazon, cheaper than Google. Every other name here is a story about what AI *will* do to costs. Meta has already filed it.
- Amazon's operating margin stalls below 14% next quarter despite the robot rollout — the savings would be one-off, not structural.

**AEHR is a judgement call worth being clear about.** Aehr makes the ovens, in effect — machines that stress-test chips while they're still on the wafer, before anyone slices them up. Historically most of its revenue came from silicon carbide chips for electric vehicles, which is why it was sitting in Chips Manufacturing. The newer and faster-growing part of the business is testing silicon-photonics and AI optical devices, which is presumably why you want it next to LITE, COHR, AAOI and now AXTI.

So the label now describes where the growth is coming from, not where the money currently comes from. That's a defensible way to organise a watchlist — but keep in mind when you look at that group that AEHR's EV exposure hasn't disappeared, and the EV chip cycle has been weak. If silicon carbide demand stays soft, AEHR can go down while the rest of the photonics shelf goes up. It won't move in sympathy with its new neighbours the way LITE and COHR move with each other.

**What AXT actually does.** Everyone in that group makes the finished optical parts — transceivers, lasers, modules. AXT makes the *plate the parts are built on*. It grows crystal wafers out of indium phosphide, gallium arsenide and germanium. Think of the group as a bakery: LITE and COHR bake the cake, AXT mills the flour. When AI data centres need far more optical links, the flour mill gets busy before anyone else does. That's exactly why it belongs where you put it.

**AEHR is a judgement call worth being clear about.** Aehr makes the ovens, in effect — machines that stress-test chips while they're still on the wafer, before anyone slices them up. Historically most of its revenue came from silicon carbide chips for electric vehicles, which is why it was sitting in Chips Manufacturing. The newer and faster-growing part of the business is testing silicon-photonics and AI optical devices, which is presumably why you want it next to LITE, COHR, AAOI and now AXTI.

So the label now describes where the growth is coming from, not where the money currently comes from. That's a defensible way to organise a watchlist — but keep in mind when you look at that group that AEHR's EV exposure hasn't disappeared, and the EV chip cycle has been weak. If silicon carbide demand stays soft, AEHR can go down while the rest of the photonics shelf goes up. It won't move in sympathy with its new neighbours the way LITE and COHR move with each other.

More importantly, it has **no revenue at all** — none, in any year since 2022. Analysts expect the company to make $50,000 in sales this entire year. That is fifty thousand dollars, not fifty million. It has 16 employees. It has $31 million in the bank and has already signed a commitment to put another $77 million into a joint venture with GE Vernova, which is a $46 million hole it has no obvious way to fill except by issuing more shares — and it's already issuing them fast, up 10% in a single quarter. It jumped 20% on Aug 3 and the financial press openly reported that nobody could find a reason why. Think of it as buying a ticket, not building a position — the size should be money you'd be relaxed about losing entirely.
| **AIRJ** | No revenue at all | GE Vernova JV live, Kubota deal | ⏸️ Interesting, not today |

I want to be fair to it, because it's the most interesting of the three rejects. AirJoule has a 50/50 joint venture with GE Vernova that is genuinely operating — they installed a unit at GE Vernova's research campus in New York on July 28. Kubota signed them as exclusive US residential partner on July 21 (the stock jumped 15% that day). They have $35M cash and no debt, funded into 2028. All five analysts covering it have targets **above** the current price — the lowest target, $6.00, sits above the $5.95 price.
